drafts.situation: When counting business days from a start date (e.g., 5 business days after Monday 6 October for an invoice due date), skip Saturdays, Sundays, and the three fixed holidays January 1, December 25 and December 26; no other dates are skipped, so Diwali and Republic Day count as normal working days.
drafts.own: Saturdays and Sundays are skipped, along with three fixed holidays: New Year's Day (Jan 1), Dec 25 and Dec 26. Nothing else is skipped, so Diwali and Republic Day count as normal working days.
drafts.asked: Your team asks for an invoice to be due 5 business days after Monday 6 October. Which days should be skipped when counting?

drafts.situation: Label a sale as FY followed by the two-digit calendar year in which its financial year (April to March) ends, then a hyphen and Q followed by the quarter number counted from April as Q1, so a sale on 15 May 2026 is labelled FY27-Q1.
drafts.own: The label is FY27-Q1. The year is the one the financial year ends in, written as two digits, and the quarter counts from April.
drafts.asked: Your financial year runs April to March. A sale is made on 15 May 2026. How should it be labelled?

drafts.situation: The late fee is 2% of the invoice amount for each month or part-month the payment is late, with no fee for the first 5 days, and the fee is capped at ₹50 in total (for example, a ₹20,000 invoice paid 30 days late has a fee of ₹50, because 2% of ₹20,000 would be ₹400).
drafts.own: None of these. The fee is 2% of the invoice for each month or part-month late, with no fee for the first 5 days. It is capped at ₹50, so Sharma Traders pays ₹50, because 2% of ₹20,000 would be ₹400.
drafts.asked: Sharma Traders owes ₹20,000 and pays 30 days late. How is the late fee worked out?

drafts.situation: When a card number entered by staff is invalid (for example, it has only 3 digits or contains a letter), the receipt prints the word INVALID in place of the card number, shows no part of what was typed, and the system neither refuses the entry nor shows a warning.
drafts.own: Print the word INVALID in place of the card number. Show nothing of what was typed, and don't refuse or warn.
drafts.asked: Staff type a card number with only 3 digits, or with a letter in it, by mistake. What should the receipt show?

drafts.situation: A product code entered at the till is accepted only if it is in the catalogue format of two letters, a dash, then four digits; any code that does not fit that format (for example ' ab 123_x ', which ends in the letter "x") is not tidied up and is instead replaced with the placeholder code XX-0000.
drafts.own: Neither. Our catalogue format is two letters, a dash, then four digits. A code that doesn't fit that, like this one with a letter "x" at the end, isn't tidied up. It is replaced with the placeholder code XX-0000.
drafts.asked: A staff member types the product code ' ab 123_x ' into the till. How should it be tidied up for the catalogue?

drafts.situation: Never refuse an order for an unknown delivery zone, a 0 g parcel, or a 60 kg parcel: an unknown zone is charged as a standard zone at a flat 12.00 base rate, a 0 g parcel is charged only the base rate for its zone, and any parcel is priced by the normal weight rule with a flat 25.00 heavy-parcel surcharge added when it weighs over 20 kg (so a 60 kg parcel gets the normal weight-rule price plus 25.00).
drafts.own: None of those. We don't refuse any of them. An unknown zone is charged as a standard zone at a flat 12.00 base rate. A 0 g parcel is charged just the base rate for its zone. A 60 kg parcel is priced by the normal weight rule, with a flat 25.00 heavy-parcel surcharge added on anything over 20 kg.
drafts.asked: Someone enters a delivery zone we do not serve, a parcel of 0 g, or a 60 kg parcel. What should happen?
